cards.heading: A VLAN is a separate broadcast domain
cards.body: VLANs split one physical switch into several logical ones. Hosts in different VLANs can't talk at layer 2; traffic between VLANs has to be routed. VLAN 1 exists by default and can't be deleted.
cards.example:
vlan 10
 name SALES
vlan 20
 name ENGINEERING

cards.heading: Access ports
cards.body: An access port belongs to exactly one VLAN and sends frames untagged. Set the mode explicitly instead of leaving the port dynamic. If the VLAN doesn't exist yet, IOS creates it for you.
cards.example:
interface range fa0/1 - 5
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10

cards.heading: Trunks and 802.1Q
cards.body: A trunk carries many VLANs between switches by adding an 802.1Q tag with the VLAN ID to each frame. Frames in the native VLAN are sent untagged; both ends must agree on it. Limit the allowed list to the VLANs you actually need.
cards.example:
interface g0/1
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk native vlan 99
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99

cards.heading: DTP: let it negotiate or not
cards.body: Ports default to dynamic auto: they become a trunk only if the other side actively asks (trunk or dynamic desirable). Two dynamic auto ports stay access ports. Best practice is to configure trunks statically and turn DTP off with 'switchport nonegotiate'. Dynamic desirable actively asks to trunk; dynamic auto only answers. A dynamic auto port acts as an access port (in VLAN 1 by default) unless the other side asks. 'switchport nonegotiate' stops DTP frames and only works with a static mode.
cards.example:
auto + auto       → access
auto + desirable  → trunk
trunk + auto      → trunk
cards.mnemonic:
Desirable is desperate: it asks to trunk. Auto is apathetic: it only answers. One asker is enough. Two auto ports both wait to be asked and stay access ports.
These are the same words PAgP uses, because both are Cisco's own protocols.

cards.heading: Verify
cards.body: 'show vlan brief' lists VLANs and their access ports (trunk ports aren't listed). 'show interfaces trunk' shows trunk mode, native VLAN and which VLANs are allowed and active. The last list in 'show interfaces trunk', VLANs in spanning tree forwarding state and not pruned, shows what the port really forwards: a VLAN allowed and active but missing there is usually blocked by STP (or pruned by VTP). 'show interfaces fa0/1 switchport' shows a port's administrative and operational mode, access and native VLAN and DTP state.
cards.example:
SW1#show interfaces trunk
Port   Mode  Encapsulation  Status    Native vlan
Gi0/1  on    802.1q         trunking  99

cards.heading: Voice VLANs and allowed lists
cards.body: An access port can also carry a voice VLAN: the PC's frames stay untagged in the access VLAN and the IP phone tags its own frames with the voice VLAN. On a trunk, 'switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20' replaces the whole list, so use 'add' or 'remove' to change it. Set the same unused native VLAN on both ends; a mismatch leaks frames between the two VLANs, and CDP reports it. The phone learns the voice VLAN through CDP. An unused native VLAN also closes VLAN hopping by double tagging: an attacker in the native VLAN sends a frame with two tags, the first switch strips the outer (native) tag and the inner tag carries it into another VLAN.
cards.example:
interface fa0/5
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10
 switchport voice vlan 20
!
interface g0/1
 switchport trunk allowed vlan add 40
 switchport trunk native vlan 99

cards.heading: VLAN numbers and the 802.1Q tag
cards.body: Normal-range VLANs are 1-1005 (1002-1005 are reserved for old Token Ring and FDDI); the extended range is 1006-4094; 0 and 4095 are reserved. VLAN 1 is the default: every port starts in it, it's the default native VLAN, and it can't be deleted or renamed. 'vlan 30' then 'name HR' creates and names a VLAN; 'interface vlan 30' creates an SVI instead. 802.1Q inserts a 4-byte tag after the source MAC: a 2-byte TPID (0x8100) and a 2-byte TCI with a 3-bit priority (PCP/CoS), 1-bit DEI and 12-bit VLAN ID. ISL was the old Cisco-proprietary method that wrapped the whole frame in a 26-byte header and 4-byte trailer; it's obsolete.
cards.mnemonic:
A 12-bit VLAN ID gives 4096 values (0-4095). The two ends are reserved, so the last usable VLAN is 4094.
Normal range ends at 1005, and its last four (1002-1005) belong to old Token Ring and FDDI.
The tag in three numbers, 4-12-3: a 4-byte tag, a 12-bit VLAN ID and a 3-bit priority. That priority is the CoS that QoS uses, values 0-7.

cards.heading: Routing between VLANs
cards.body: Each VLAN is its own subnet, so hosts in different VLANs need a layer 3 device. Hosts in the same VLAN on two switches don't need routing, but the link between the switches must carry that VLAN. Router-on-a-stick uses one router port on a switch trunk with a subinterface per VLAN. A multilayer switch uses an SVI per VLAN, and needs 'ip routing'; without it the SVIs only work as management addresses.
cards.example:
interface g0/0.10
 encapsulation dot1Q 10
 ip address 10.1.10.1 255.255.255.0
!
ip routing
interface vlan 20
 ip address 10.1.20.1 255.255.255.0
